title: MaxSup: Overcoming Representation Collapse in Label Smoothing

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 3.3 states 'L_LS ≈ α(z_gt − (1/K)∑z_k) − log∑_j e^{z_j}', but Appendix B's proof of this exact theorem derives 'L_LS = α(z_gt − (1/K)∑z_k)' with no log-sum-exp term (Eq. 18, and the subsequent derivation in Eqs. 19–26). The extra '−log∑e^{z_j}' term in the main-text theorem contradicts its own proof and is also inconsistent with Corollary 3.4, which is built from the term without the log-sum-exp component.

Corollary 3.4 decomposes L_LS using a uniform coefficient α/K for both the regularization term (∑_{z_m<z_gt}) and the error-amplification term (∑_{z_n>z_gt}): L_LS = (α/K)∑(z_gt−z_m) + (α/K)∑(z_gt−z_n). However, Table 1 tests 'Regularization' as (α/M)∑(z_gt−z_m) and 'error amplification' as (α/N)∑(z_gt−z_n), using M and N (counts of logits below/above z_gt) instead of K in the denominator. This changes the scaling of each term relative to the theoretically derived decomposition, so the ablation in Table 1 does not actually isolate the two components as defined by Eq. (5), undermining the claimed direct correspondence between the theory and the ablation results.

The text states 'We further investigate MaxSup's applicability to downstream tasks by evaluating its performance on semantic segmentation using the widely adopted MMSegmentation framework [6].' However, reference [6] in the bibliography is 'Yingbo Gao et al., Towards a better understanding of label smoothing in neural machine translation' — a paper about label smoothing in NMT, not the MMSegmentation toolbox. This is also the same reference number used earlier in the Introduction for NMT applications of LS ('neural machine translation [1, 6]'), confirming the segmentation-framework citation is misattributed.

Table 13 lists a row 'Logit Normalization [3*]' with accuracy 74.32. The surrounding text explicitly attributes this method and the 74.32% accuracy to reference [38] ('the method proposed in [38] aims to mitigate overconfidence via logit normalization... achieves an accuracy of 74.32%'). Reference [3] in the bibliography is 'Shiming Chen et al., HSVA: Hierarchical semantic-visual adaptation for zero-shot learning', which is unrelated to logit normalization. The table citation number does not match the reference actually discussed in text.

The text states 'Notably, MaxSup maintains d̄_within reductions similar to other methods, suggesting only marginal benefits in preserving intra-class statistics.' However, Table 2 shows MaxSup's d̄_within (0.293 train / 0.300 val) is substantially closer to the baseline (0.311/0.331) than LS (0.263/0.254), OLS (0.271/0.282), or Zipf-LS (0.261/0.293), indicating MaxSup preserves intra-class variation noticeably better than the other LS-based methods, not 'similarly'. This directly conflicts with the paper's central claim elsewhere (Abstract, Figure 1, Section 1) that MaxSup substantially restores intra-class variation.

The Impact paragraph states 'we have not observed any additional adverse effects or trade-offs.' This directly contradicts the paper's own reported findings: Table 7 shows MaxSup fails on minority ('Low') classes in long-tailed classification (0.0% accuracy, same as baselines, explicitly called a 'fairness concern'); Table 8 shows MaxSup has worse NLL (1.770) than LS (1.476) on CIFAR-10-C; and the preceding paragraph of the same Conclusion section explicitly states 'some scenarios—such as severe class imbalance and out-of-distribution evaluation—highlight residual challenges and limitations.'

Section 4.2.1 claims: 'hyperparameters and training settings are re-tuned under each training recipe to ensure optimal performance for each method... This re-tuning guarantees that reported performance differences reflect method improvements rather than hyperparameter bias.' However, Section 4.2.2 states the opposite regarding OLS and Zipf-LS: 'we apply the authors' official codebases and hyperparameters but do not replicate their complete training recipes (e.g., OLS trains for 250 epochs... Zipf-LS uses 100 epochs...). Even under these modified settings, MaxSup remains robust.' This is a direct contradiction about whether baseline methods were fairly/fully tuned, undermining the fairness claim made in 4.2.1.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2.2, Long-Tailed Classification discussion of Table 7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'MaxSup achieves a better trade-off between many- and medium-shot accuracy,' but Table 7 shows this does not hold uniformly: for the test split at imbalance ratio 50, MaxSup's medium-shot accuracy (73.4) is lower than LS's (75.4), contradicting the generalized claim of a consistently better trade-off.
